newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM dismisses Murdoch "backwater" attack.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM dismisses Murdoch "backwater" attack.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard hit back at Rupert Murdoch on Thursday after the powerful media magnate said Australia risked becoming an economic backwater without radical reforms.

In two separate attacks this week, Australia-born Murdoch criticised the pace of reform in the first nine months of Howard's conservative government and held up neighbouring New Zealand as a model to be followed.

"Unless we hurry up and do something with our tax system and our whole structure, we cannot live in Asia as a full partner of Asian countries," Murdoch told Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) television in Tokyo on Wednesday.
Howard reacted angrily, telling ABC radio on Thursday: "I think the remarks Rupert made indicate just how disconnected he's becoming with Australia."

"Anybody who has been in Australia over the past few months, particularly the past couple of months, and has really followed things closely could barely say that we haven't achieved some quite fundamental reforms."

Murdoch, now a U.S. citizen but still controlling Australia's largest media empire, said the country needed tax reforms and deeper industrial relations reform. He said gun law changes after April's Port Arthur massacre and the recent race debate had distracted Howard's conservative coalition.
"Australia really has to have some pretty radical rebuilding if we are not going to become a backwater," Murdoch said.
"I think we are at real risk of becoming a backwater unless we hurry up and get some energy into the country much the same way New Zealand did."
Howard, whose March 2 election victory ended 13 years of Labor Party rule, replied: "I was fascinated by his comment that we were distracted by the guns debate.
"Yes, I was. I plead guilty to that. I think the Australian public wanted me to be distracted by that. They, in fact, didn't regard it as a distraction."

Howard also denied that Australia had been subjected to a racism debate, saying controversy in the past three months over immigration levels was a response to independent politician Pauline Hanson's first speech to parliament.
During that speech in early September, Hanson warned Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.

"We've not had a race debate -- we've had a debate about responses to a speech -- and nobody in the government, nobody in the opposition, nobody is seriously arguing that we should go back to the White Australia policy," Howard said.
"I've made it very clear that under no circumstances is that going to happen," he said.
